sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**

None. Every line in this section is a yes. Two copy problems have no checklist line of their own, so I list them here for the director to weigh:

1. **No checklist line: the article never says how to change the card.**
   - **Where:** the H1 at about x 380–912, y 135–210 reads "Update the card that pays for your subscription", which promises a task. The body at y 235–620 gives policy instead: who may change the card, when the new card is charged, and what happens when it is declined. The only directions are "from the billing page" (y 247), with no link, no menu path and no steps. Yet four other phrases are links.
   - **What the viewer meets:** a reader who came to do the task finishes the page still not knowing where to click. They have to go and find the billing page themselves, or contact support.
   - **Why:** this is the job of a how-to help article. Krug, *Don't Make Me Think*, says the page should make the next action self-evident. Applied to missing steps, that is my judgment.
   - **Fix:** link "the billing page" and add a short numbered path, such as Settings → Billing → Payment method → Replace card, before the policy paragraphs. Or retitle the page to match what it actually covers.
   - **Type and weight:** defect, major.

2. **No checklist line: the dates and outcomes the viewer will act on can be read two ways.**
   - **Where:** the paragraph under "When the new card is declined" (y 515–620), plus one line in the first paragraph.
   - "after three days and after seven days" does not say what the days count from: the first decline, or each other. So a retry could be on day 7 or day 10.
   - "after the second attempt" could mean the second retry (day 7) or the first retry, if the original charge counts as attempt one (day 3). On the second reading the plan drops four days sooner than the reader expects.
   - In the first paragraph, "any invoice that is already open keeps the old card until it is paid" doesn't say what happens when the old card is the one that is failing. That is the most common reason anyone is on this page.
   - **What the viewer meets:** these are the deadlines and consequences a customer plans around and later holds the company to. A wrong reading means a surprise downgrade or an invoice that is never paid.
   - **Fix:** anchor the dates to one event and name the outcome. For example: "We retry 3 days and 7 days after the first decline. If the day-7 retry fails, your subscription moves to the free plan." Also say what happens to an open invoice when the old card can't pay it.
   - **Type and weight:** defect, major.

**What's working.**
- **One voice throughout:** one sans family in two weights, one link blue and plenty of white space. The page reads as a single calm, trustworthy whole, which suits a billing topic where people are often anxious.
- **Plain, second-person copy:** lines like "Your workspace stays open during this period" tell the reader the consequence for them, not just how the system behaves. That is the reassurance someone with a declined card needs first.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether "Update a payment card" in the left list (x 96–251, y 178) shows as the current page in the live site. In this capture it looks identical to the other items. That belongs to the interface section.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The title clearly leads.** The H1 "Update the card that pays for your subscription" (about x 380–912, y 135–212) is the largest and boldest text on the page. The eye lands on it first and learns right away what the page is for. Nothing in the header or sidebar competes with it: the "Ledgerly Help" logo and the nav links are much smaller and lighter.
- **Each level of text has its own job.** The heading "When the new card is declined" (y≈487) looks only about 2 px larger than the 17 px body text, but it is bold where the body is regular. That makes the difference obvious at a glance, which is the test in Dair, *Design with Type*, ch. 8. The 13 px grey breadcrumb and the "In this section" label sit clearly below the body text. That gives three readable levels in the content (title, heading, body) plus one smaller level for navigation. Keep the bold weight on the H2: it is the only thing separating it from the body text. If the H2 were ever set in regular weight, it would read as an accident.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The page runs on one clear set of column lines.** The logo and the "In this section" list share a left edge at about x=96. The top-nav links end at about x=1184, which gives the right margin. The article column starts at x=380, and the breadcrumb, title, body and subhead all hang from that line. The breadcrumb and "In this section" sit on the same baseline (y≈113), which ties the two columns together. The reader sees one plan, not blocks placed one at a time (Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems*). Keep these shared lines when the page gets longer content, a callout or a screenshot.
- **The spacing shows how the content groups.** The gap above "When the new card is declined" (about 34 px from the last line of the paragraph above) is roughly twice the gap below it (about 18 px). That makes the subhead belong to the text it introduces. The extra space between paragraphs (about 18 px on top of a 28 px line pitch) separates the paragraphs without breaking the column apart. The empty space is in three large areas: under the sidebar, to the right of the article, and below the article. It isn't scattered in small leftover gaps, so the page reads as calm and easy to scan, which is right for a help article.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- How the two columns reflow at tablet and phone widths. A help article like this is often opened from an email on a phone. Check whether the sidebar moves above the article or collapses, and whether the 96 px margins shrink in proportion.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 13 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

**Text: applies.** The type is in good shape. Two lines fail: body lines run a bit long, and the main heading wraps in an awkward place. Both are minor.

**Findings**
1. **Do paragraph lines run about 45 to 75 characters?** No. Body paragraphs at x 380–1050 hold about 80–85 characters per line. For example, "You can replace the card on file at any time from the billing page. The new card is" is about 83. On a page that is mostly long paragraphs, the eye has a little further to travel back to the start of each next line. The large type (~17 px) and loose line spacing (~28 px) make this easier. Bringhurst gives 45 to 75 characters as the comfortable range (*The Elements of Typographic Style*, 2.1.2). To fix it, narrow the text column to about 600–620 px at this size, which gives roughly 66 characters. The empty right margin past x 1050 has room to keep the column where it is. *Convention. Minor.* Measure the real characters-per-line in a browser to confirm.
2. **Do headings and captions break at phrase boundaries?** No. The H1 (x 380–912, y 135–212) breaks as "Update the card that pays for your / subscription". This separates "your" from its noun and leaves one word on the second line, so the heading reads as a long line with a leftover word rather than as one statement. No confirmed source covers breaks in headings, so this is common sense. To fix it, break before "for your subscription", or shorten the heading to "Update your payment card", which also matches the sidebar item. *Taste. Minor.*

**What's working.**
- **Type scale.** There are four clear levels: H1 ~32 px bold, H3 ~19 px semibold, body ~17 px, and labels ~13–15 px. All use one sans family, so each size has an obvious job and nothing collides.
- **Body text is easy to read.** It is larger than the nav and sidebar text, near-black on white, with generous line spacing and short paragraphs broken up by a subhead. A user who is worried about billing can scan it easily.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 28 yes, 2 no (lines of 45 to 75 characters; heading breaks at phrase boundaries)

The color review is done. The one problem is the links in the body text, which are marked by color alone.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is every meaning shown by color (status, category, a marked item) also shown by a label, icon, pattern, or position?** No.
   - **Where:** the four inline links in the article body. They are "check your billing history" (about x 863–1005, y 303 and x 380–435, y 331), "roles and permissions" (x 606–783, y 405), "paying by invoice" (x 752–893, y 433) and "restore your previous plan" (x 414–624, y 609).
   - **What the viewer meets:** these links are only a medium blue against near-black body text. They have no underline, no change in weight and no icon. A reader with a color-vision deficiency, a low-quality screen or bright glare may not see them as links. That matters here, because this text sends people to the next step: checking billing history first, or getting the billing role. The blue and the near-black are both dark, so they look close in lightness. By eye the difference looks under the 3:1 that WCAG allows as a color-only alternative for links. Check this with a contrast tool, comparing the link color to the body text color.
   - **Why:** WCAG 2.2, SC 1.4.1 Use of Color. Failure technique F73 says that leaving only a color difference for links in running text is a failure.
   - **Fix:** underline the links inside paragraphs, or give them another mark besides color, so that a reader who can't tell the colors apart can still find them.
   - **Type and weight:** defect (also a published convention). Major for a help article whose links are the way into related tasks.

**What's working.**
- **Restrained palette:** the page uses one neutral range (near-black for the headline and body, mid-gray for the breadcrumb, sidebar and "In this section" label, a light gray rule under the header) and one hue, used only for links. Every bit of color on the page means "you can click this", which suits a help page that someone reads under some stress about billing.
- **Clear light and dark range:** the near-black headline, dark body text and lighter gray navigation separate article from nav by value alone. The structure still holds in grayscale.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- **Link hover and focus:** WCAG's other way to pass for links only works if hover and focus add a cue other than color, such as an underline. That needs checking in a live browser.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 8 yes, 1 no (meaning shown by color also shown another way).

**Section.** Pictures: skipped. The page has no photos, illustrations or icons. "Ledgerly Help" at the top left (about x 96–218, y 22–42) is plain bold text with no drawn mark, so it belongs under Text, not here.

**Findings**
None.

**Checklist.** Pictures: skipped

sections.report:
**Walk (working notes): Interface**

The image is 1280×800, about one screen, so I worked from the whole image. Bash was refused, so I could not run the crop and entries scripts.

First read: the eye lands on the H1 "Update the card that pays for your subscription", then drops to the body. This is a help-centre article for a SaaS billing customer. It is calm and plain. The controls are the top nav, the side nav, the breadcrumb and the inline links.

1. One primary button: yes (there are no buttons on the page).
2. Controls look like what they do, links marked by more than colour: **no**. The inline links are blue with no underline, inside body text.
3. Non-text contrast 3:1: yes (no fields or icons).
4. Hover, pressed and disabled states shown: yes (none shown).
5. Focus indicator: unsure (can't tell from a still).
6. Focus left uncovered: unsure (can't tell from a still).
7. Main content left uncovered: yes.
8. Targets large enough: yes. The side nav rows are about 31 px apart.
9. Phone thumb zone: yes (n/a, this is desktop).
10. Shows where the user is: **no**. "Update a payment card" in the side nav and "Billing" in the top nav have no current-page marker. Only the breadcrumb tells you where you are.
11. A way out: yes.
12. to 21. Form and error lines: yes (n/a).
22. Empty states: yes (n/a).
23. Help near the step: yes (the page is the help).
24. Shortcuts: **no**. A help centre with no search anywhere.
25. Puts the next thing in front of the user: **no**. "From the billing page" is not a link, and the page has no steps for changing the card.
26. Conventions: yes. This is the familiar docs layout, apart from the missing search, which is filed under line 24.
27. Audience's words: yes.
28. Link purpose: yes.
29. Sensory instructions: yes.
30. Conceptual model: yes.
31. Consistency across screens: yes (one screen).
32. Reflow: yes.
33. Honest choices: yes.

The entries could not be opened (Bash denied), so the deep read uses the rule summaries in critic.md.

**Section.** Interface: applies. The page has a top nav, a side nav, a breadcrumb and inline links. There are no buttons or forms, so 13 lines (forms, errors, empty states, destructive actions, thumb zone, states, dialogs) are met by default.

**Findings**
1. **Does the screen put what the user likely needs next in front of them (a prefilled default, the next action, or the information they came for) instead of making them hunt for it?** No.
   - **Where:** the first paragraph (y≈247), "You can replace the card on file at any time from the billing page."
   - **What the viewer meets:** this is the one action the reader came for. Yet "the billing page" is plain text, while the side trips ("check your billing history", "roles and permissions", "paying by invoice") are links. The article also never says how to change the card: there are no steps and no button name. The title promises "Update the card…", but the reader leaves without the path and has to hunt for the billing page and the right control from memory.
   - **Why:** Tognazzini's "Anticipation" (off-list source, so I argue it on its own terms) and Nielsen 6, "Recognition rather than recall".
   - **Fix:** link "the billing page" straight to the screen where the card is changed. Give the short sequence of steps, naming the real controls ("Settings → Billing → Payment method → Replace card"). A "Go to billing" button at the top would also work.
   - **Kind:** defect. **Weight:** major.
2. **Does the screen show where the user is and what is happening, such as the current page or step, progress, or loading?** No.
   - **Where:** the side nav at x≈96–251, y≈147–271. "Update a payment card" (y≈178) looks the same as its siblings. "Billing" in the top nav (x≈792) is not marked either.
   - **What the viewer meets:** only the small grey breadcrumb (y≈113) says where they are. The side nav label also differs from the H1 ("Update a payment card" against "Update the card that pays for your subscription"), so the reader has to work out which nav item they are on.
   - **Why:** Nielsen 1, "Visibility of system status".
   - **Fix:** give the current side-nav item and the current top-nav section a clear active state, using weight, a bar, or a tint, not colour alone. Matching the nav label to the H1 also helps.
   - **Kind:** convention. **Weight:** minor.
3. **Does every control look like what it does, buttons pressable, fields typeable, and links marked by more than color?** No.
   - **Where:** the four inline links in the body: "check your billing history" (y≈303–331), "roles and permissions" (y≈405), "paying by invoice" (y≈433) and "restore your previous plan" (y≈609).
   - **What the viewer meets:** these links are marked by blue alone, with no underline, and the body text is near-black. Colour-blind readers, and anyone on a low-quality display, may not see them as links.
   - **Why:** WCAG 1.4.1 (Use of Color). The colour-only route needs 3:1 contrast between the link and the surrounding text, plus a non-colour cue on hover or focus. That has to be measured, and dark blue against near-black is unlikely to reach 3:1.
   - **Fix:** underline links in running text. The nav and side-nav links can stay plain, since their position already marks them.
   - **Kind:** convention. **Weight:** minor.
4. **Are shortcuts offered for frequent actions, such as search, filters, or keyboard hints?** No.
   - **Where:** the header (y 0–63). It has a logo and four nav links but no search.
   - **What the viewer meets:** most help-centre visitors arrive with a question in their own words. Without search, they have to guess which of the four top-level sections holds their answer and then scan the lists inside it. Search is also the convention for help centres (Jakob's law).
   - **Why:** Nielsen 7, "Flexibility and efficiency of use".
   - **Fix:** add a search field in the header, visible on every article.
   - **Kind:** convention. **Weight:** major. For a help site, search is the main way in.

**What's working.**
- The link text is descriptive ("roles and permissions", "paying by invoice"), not "click here", so each link's purpose is clear from its words. Keep that.
- "Contact support" sits in the top nav on every page, so the way out of a dead end is always visible.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Focus indicators on the nav and inline links.
- Whether the links get an underline or another non-colour cue on hover or focus. That decides whether finding 3 fails WCAG 1.4.1.
- Whether the breadcrumb items are links.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 27 yes, 4 no (links marked by more than colour; shows where the user is; shortcuts such as search; puts what the user needs next in front of them), 2 unsure (focus indicator; focus not obscured).

The scripts didn't run because Bash was refused. I worked from the whole image without crops (it is about one screen, so no crops were needed) and didn't open the reference entries for the four "no" lines. The fix directions and sources above come from the rule summaries in critic.md, not the full entries.
